findings.summary: Interface 'Models' row and the code example appear before the idea is stated, and the Protocol bullet claims 'Neither' covers ABC and Protocol, which is inaccurate (a Protocol class can be instantiated only if it is a non-protocol subclass; direct Protocol instantiation raises TypeError, but the claim mixes structural and nominal semantics).
findings.evidence:

findings.summary: Page 2 uses default methods and MRO before either is defined or explained.
findings.evidence: "Lookup order | explicit override | MRO (C3 linearization)" and "interface Flyer { default void move() {} }" appear on page 2, while default methods are only introduced on page 3, and MRO is never spelled out as method resolution order.
findings.fix: Add one line on page 2 before the diamond section: a Java default method is an interface method with a body, and MRO (method resolution order) is the order Python searches base classes for a method. Or move page 3's default-method intro ahead of the diamond.

findings.summary: The Duck example is a code listing with a stray prose fragment and the 'Why Interfaces Stack' section is a prose paragraph holding several ideas.
findings.evidence: Java forbids multiple inheritance of state, so you extend one abstract class. Interfaces carry no state, so one class can hold many capabilities.
findings.fix: Split into bullets: 'Java: one superclass only (no multiple state)', 'Interfaces have no state', 'So a class can implement many interfaces'.
